'''Troy Davis''' (born September 14, 1975) is an American former professional [[gridiron football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) and [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Iowa State Cyclones football|Iowa State Cyclones]], finishing as a finalist for the [[Heisman Trophy]]. Davis twice earned consensus [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] honors and was the first and one of only two [[NCAA Division I-A]] running backs to rush for over 2,000 yards in back-to-back seasons. In 2016, he was inducted into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]].<ref name=cfbhof/> He played professionally for the [[New Orleans Saints]] of the NFL, and the [[Hamilton Tiger-Cats]], [[Edmonton Eskimos]] and [[Toronto Argonauts]] of the CFL, and was a member of the Eskimos' [[Grey Cup]] championship team in 2005.

'''Troy Kenneth Aikman''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|eɪ|k|m|ən}}; born November 21, 1966)<ref name="hall of" /><ref>{{Cite web |date=May 31, 2023 |title=Troy Aikman |url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Troy-Aikman |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230516144410/https://www.britannica.com/biography/Troy-Aikman |archive-date=May 16, 2023 |access-date=May 31, 2023 |website=[[Encyclopedia Britannica]]}}</ref> is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[quarterback]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 12 seasons with the [[Dallas Cowboys]]. After transferring from the [[Oklahoma Sooners football|Oklahoma Sooners]], he played [[college football]] for the [[UCLA Bruins football|UCLA Bruins]] and won the [[Davey O'Brien Award]] as a senior. Aikman was selected [[List of first overall NFL draft picks|first overall]] in the [[1989 NFL draft]] by the Cowboys, where he was named to six [[Pro Bowl]]s and won three [[Super Bowl]]s. He was also named [[Super Bowl Most Valuable Player|MVP]] of [[Super Bowl XXVII]], the franchise's first title in over a decade. Aikman was inducted to the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in 2006<ref name="hall of">{{cite web|url=http://www.profootballhof.com/hof/member.aspx?PLAYER_ID=254|title=Hall of Famers|publisher=Pro Football Hall of Fame|year=2006|access-date=April 19, 2010|archive-date=October 2, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151002011741/http://www.profootballhof.com/hof/member.aspx?PLAYER_ID=254|url-status=dead}}</ref> and the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 2008.

After retiring in 2000, Aikman served as the [[color commentator]] of ''[[NFL on Fox]]'' from 2001 to 2021 and has served as the color commentator of ''[[Monday Night Football]]'' on [[ESPN]] and [[ESPN on ABC|ABC]] since 2022. He and his partner [[Sports commentator|play-by-play announcer]] [[Joe Buck]] are the longest tenured announcer pairing in NFL history.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Reedy |first=Joe |date=November 8, 2023 |title=Buck and Aikman are now the longest-tenured broadcast crew in NFL history |url=https://apnews.com/article/nfl-monday-night-football-buck-aikman-2bb6a91e9f72196c2461ae6243bc07fd |access-date=February 20, 2024 |website=AP News |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Curtis |first=Bryan |date=September 11, 2023 |title=22 Years of Joe Buck and Troy Aikman |url=https://www.theringer.com/2023/09/11/nfl/joe-buck-troy-aikman-22-years-nfl-announcers |website=www.theringer.com |access-date=January 10, 2025}}</ref> Aikman was a co-owner of the now defunct NASCAR [[Sprint Cup Series]] team [[Hall of Fame Racing]] from 2005 to 2009, along with fellow former Cowboys quarterback [[Roger Staubach]], and is also a part-owner of the [[San Diego Padres]] in [[Major League Baseball]] (MLB).<ref>{{cite web | last=Page | first=Eric S. | url=https://www.nbcsandiego.com/news/sports/New-Padres-Owners-Take-the-Field.html | title=New Padres Owners Take the Field | publisher=NBC San Diego | date=July 17, 2009 | access-date=September 20, 2010}}</ref><ref>{{cite news | last=Center | first=Bill | url=https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/sports/padres/sdut-padres-sold-group-headed-omalley-heirs-2012aug06-htmlstory.html | title=Padres sold to group headed by O'Malley heirs | newspaper=[[San Diego Union-Tribune]] | date=August 6, 2012 | access-date=June 27, 2017}}</ref>

'''Troy Edwards''' (born April 7, 1977) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] for seven seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).  He played [[college football]] for the [[Louisiana Tech Bulldogs football|Louisiana Tech Bulldogs]], became one of the most prolific receivers in college football history. He earned [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] honors and won the [[Fred Biletnikoff Award]]. Edwards was selected by the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] in the first round of the [[1999 NFL draft]], and played for the Steelers, [[St. Louis Rams]], [[Jacksonville Jaguars]], and [[Detroit Lions]] of the NFL. He also played for the [[Grand Rapids Rampage]] of the [[Arena Football League (1987–2008)|Arena Football League]] (AFL).

'''Sullivan Anthony''' "'''Tripp'''" '''Welborne III''' (born November 20, 1968) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player for the [[Minnesota Vikings]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL).

Welborne played [[college football]], principally as a [[Safety (football position)|safety]] and [[punt returner]], for the [[Michigan Wolverines football|University of Michigan]] from 1987 to 1990. He had five [[interception]]s as a sophomore in 1988, and was a two-time [[unanimous All-American]] in both 1989 and 1990, the only player in school history to do so. As a senior, he was awarded College Defensive Player of the Year, Team Most Valuable Player, and set a Michigan single-season record with 455 [[punt return]] yards (a record that stood until broken by [[Steve Breaston]] in 2003) and averaged 14.7 yards per return.

Welborne sustained a serious injury in the 10th game of the 1990 season that required reconstructive surgery on his right knee.  He was unable to play during the [[1991 NFL season]], but attempted a comeback the following year. He appeared in only two games for [[Minnesota Vikings]] during the [[1991 NFL season|1992 NFL season]] before suffering a career ending ACL injury to his left knee.
